description: WB25 is the best water based paver sealer for a wet look and Techniseal Matte for a natural one. 6 low-odor picks, plus the weather rules that stop haze.

intro: The best water based paver sealer for most patios is Foundation Armor WB25 if you want a wet look, and Techniseal Matte Finish if you want the pavers to look untouched. Both are low odor, clean up with water and are legal to buy in every state.

Water-based sealers have one real weakness: weather. They need warm, dry air to cure clear, and a coat put down on a damp evening can turn milky and stay that way. This page ranks six water-based options by finish and job, then covers the weather window, sealing over old coats and polymeric sand, pool and porcelain pavers, and how to keep the finish from clouding.
quickAnswer: For a wet look without solvent fumes, use Foundation Armor WB25. For no visible change, use Techniseal Matte or a water-based penetrant such as Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500, the best pick where winters bring snow and salt. For loose joint sand, SEK Surebond SB-6000 or Rain Guard Blok-Guard. Apply thin coats on dry pavers when it is 55 to 85 degrees Fahrenheit and dry for the next 24 hours.

sections.h: The 6 Best Water Based Paver Sealers in 2026 at a Glance

blocks.p: Water-based paver sealers come in two families. Acrylics form a thin film that adds color, sheen and joint stabilization. Penetrating repellents soak in and leave no film, so they never peel but add no color. Pick the family by the look you want, then pick the product by your joints and climate.
If you are open to solvent products too, our main [paver sealer rankings](/best-paver-sealer/) include solvent wet-look and natural stone options.

sections.h: The 6 Best Water Based Paver Sealers in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: All six are water-borne, so every one is low odor, cleans up with water and can be sold in every state. They are ranked on what the makers publish (chemistry, finish, approved surfaces, recoat and cure directions) and on what owners repeatedly report. They were not put through trials of our own.

blocks.h3: Best Overall: Foundation Armor WB25 Wet Look Acrylic

blocks.p: WB25 is the water-based answer for people who want the darker, richer wet-look color but cannot buy, or do not want to breathe, a solvent sealer. On concrete pavers it deepens color clearly and dries to a satin-to-semi-gloss sheen, a touch less glassy than Foundation Armor's solvent AR350. The odor is mild enough to work next to open windows, and rollers and sprayers rinse out with water. The label asks for thin coats on a clean, dry surface within a moderate temperature band, and that last instruction carries real weight. Water-based acrylic needs warmth and low humidity to fuse into a clear film; put it on heavy or on a damp day and it can dry milky, and a cured coat will not re-dissolve the way solvent acrylic does. Owners commonly report the best results from two light coats applied in the afternoon after several dry days.
**Pros:** real wet-look color without solvent fumes; satin-to-semi-gloss sheen; easy water cleanup; legal everywhere.
**Cons:** unforgiving of damp or cool days; mistakes mean stripping; slightly softer gloss than solvent.

blocks.h3: Best Natural-Look Acrylic: Techniseal Matte Finish Paver Sealer

blocks.p: Techniseal's matte sealer is for owners who like how their pavers look right now and only want them easier to keep clean. It dries without noticeable shine and keeps the paver close to its original tone while adding resistance to food spills, leaf tannins and everyday grime. Because it is formulated for interlocking pavers, it is also meant to help hold the top of the joint sand. That makes it a good match for a backyard patio around a grill or dining table, where grease and spilled drinks are the threat and a glossy film would look out of place. Techniseal is a name many hardscape contractors already know from jointing sand and paver cleaners, so the matching prep products are easy to find. It will not restore color that UV has bleached out; for chalky pavers, choose an enhancing product. Clean first, let the pavers dry completely and stay inside the label's temperature range.
**Pros:** no visible sheen; stain resistance for dining areas; helps hold joint sand; from a paver-focused brand.
**Cons:** no color revival; same weather sensitivity as any water-based film.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Techniseal+Matte+Finish+Paver+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Joint Sand: SEK Surebond SB-6000

blocks.p: SEK Surebond has sold paver sealers to installers for decades, and SB-6000 is its water-based product for interlocking pavers. The selling point is the joints. Flooded into dry, full joint sand, it soaks down and binds the top layer of grains, which slows washout from storms and hose-downs and makes it harder for weeds and ants to move in. On the paver faces it gives a moderate color boost with a low sheen. It is a practical choice for an older patio with ordinary sand joints, where digging out and re-sanding with polymeric would be a big job. Its weak point is shared by every joint-stabilizing sealer: it only works on a joint that is full and dry. Top up the sand, sweep the faces clean, wait for a dry stretch and expect to use noticeably more product than the paver faces alone would need.
**Pros:** binds ordinary joint sand; moderate color enhancement; low sheen; long installer track record.
**Cons:** useless on low or damp joints; high product use when flooding joints.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=SEK+Surebond+SB-6000&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Budget: Eagle Natural Seal Penetrating Sealer

blocks.p: Eagle Natural Seal is a water-based penetrating sealer stocked at many home centers, and it is the low-cost route to basic water repellency. It soaks into concrete, brick and pavers, leaves no visible film and makes water bead instead of soaking in. That slows freeze-thaw damage, salt absorption and the dark water staining you see on untreated pavers after rain. With nothing on the surface, it cannot peel, yellow or make a pool deck slippery, and a later recoat needs no stripping. You do not get any color boost or joint stabilization, and its protection is not expected to last as long as premium silane-siloxane blends that cost several times more. For a front walk or side path where you only want the pavers to stay cleaner and drier, that is a fair trade. Saturate clean, dry pavers and spread out puddles before they dry.
**Pros:** inexpensive; invisible; no peeling or added slip; easy recoat; widely sold.
**Cons:** no color or joint benefit; shorter service life than premium penetrants.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Eagle+Natural+Seal+Penetrating+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Freeze-Thaw Climates: Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500

blocks.p: In snow country, a water-based penetrant beats any acrylic film on a paver driveway, and Siloxa-Tek 8500 is Ghostshield's siloxane built for that job. Driveway pavers take tire scrub, shovel blades and de-icer; a film wears through in the tracks and leaves a patchy surface, while a penetrant has nothing on top to wear. The siloxane cuts how much water and salt brine the paver absorbs, and that absorption is what drives spalling and surface scaling over the years. Ghostshield describes it as breathable and water-based, it leaves the paver looking untreated and it does not change traction. Being breathable also makes it a reasonable choice on clay brick and many natural stones. It will not enhance color or lock joint sand, so pair it with polymeric sand if the joints wash out. Seal in fall, on dry pavers, before the first de-icer goes down.
**Pros:** strongest freeze-thaw and salt defense here; no film to wear; breathable; no slip change.
**Cons:** no color boost; does not bind sand; higher cost per gallon than budget penetrants.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ghostshield+Siloxa-Tek+8500&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Stain-Prone Patios: Rain Guard Blok-Guard

blocks.p: Blok-Guard comes from Rain Guard, a water-repellent brand, and it is marketed for interlocking pavers with an added graffiti-control claim. On a family patio that means easier cleanup of sidewalk chalk, markers, grill grease and spilled soda. It dries to a natural-to-satin finish with modest color enhancement, so the pavers look clean rather than glossy. On the first coat, flood it into dry joint sand and it binds the top of the joints, which slows washout and cuts down on weeding. The low odor is a real advantage next to a kitchen door or a play area. Expect higher product use on rough or tumbled pavers, and make sure the joints are full and dry before you start. If you want maximum color pop, this is the wrong product; if kids, a grill and a busy back door are the reality, it fits well.
**Pros:** graffiti and stain resistance; joint stabilization; subtle finish; low odor near living areas.
**Cons:** modest color only; heavy use on porous pavers; joints must be dry and full.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Rain+Guard+Blok-Guard+Paver+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: Is Water-Based or Solvent-Based Paver Sealer Better?

blocks.h3: Why most homeowners should start water-based

blocks.p: A patio sits next to doors, windows, a kitchen and often a garden, a pool or a dog run. Solvent sealers fill that space with xylene vapor for hours, call for an organic-vapor respirator and stay flammable until they flash off. Water-based sealers smell mild, rinse off tools with a hose and can go down without turning the house into a fume chamber.

California, much of the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic and a growing list of local air districts cap VOCs in coatings. Many solvent paver sealers are not sold there or are sold in weaker versions. Water-based products are legal everywhere, so the one you research is the one you can actually buy.

blocks.h3: Where solvent still has an edge

blocks.p: Solvent acrylics give a slightly deeper gloss, tolerate cool days better and can be re-melted to fix a bad coat. Water-based acrylics have closed most of the gap on stain resistance and color, but they still trail on those three points.

sections.h: What Are the Types of Water-Based Paver Sealer?

blocks.p: These are tiny acrylic particles suspended in water. As the water evaporates, the particles crowd together and fuse into a clear film on the paver face and, when flooded, in the joint sand. Acrylics deliver the sheen, the color and the joint stabilization. WB25, SB-6000, Blok-Guard and Techniseal Matte are all acrylics tuned for different looks.

Silanes, siloxanes or siliconates carried in water soak into the paver, react inside the pores and leave a water-shedding lining. Nothing sits on top, so nothing peels and nothing gets slippery, and a recoat never needs stripping. Siloxa-Tek 8500 and Eagle Natural Seal belong here. Searches for a penetrating, water-based sealer for pavers usually mean this group.

Some products blend acrylic with polyurethane for a tougher film; others are penetrating enhancers that soak in while carrying resin that darkens the paver. They cost more and are rarer at big-box stores, but they solve a specific problem, such as richer color on a driveway where a film would wear away.

H&C, a Sherwin-Williams brand sold at its paint stores, offers water-based paver sealers in natural and wet-look versions. Judge it the same way as any product above: read whether the label describes a film-forming acrylic or a penetrant, check the stated temperature range and recoat window, and confirm pavers are on the approved surface list. The type matters more than the brand; two acrylics from different makers behave more alike than an acrylic and a penetrant from the same maker.

sections.h: Can a Water Based Paver Sealer Give a Wet Look?

blocks.p: A water-based wet-look acrylic such as WB25 deepens color clearly and adds a satin-to-semi-gloss sheen. It is usually a little softer than a solvent wet look, which many owners prefer on a patio because a mirror shine shows every scuff.

blocks.h3: How to get the most color

blocks.p: Apply two thin coats rather than one heavy coat. The second coat, once the first is dry to the touch and within the label's recoat window, is what builds depth. A heavy single coat looks wetter for an hour and then dries cloudy.

blocks.h3: Where a wet look is a bad idea

blocks.p: Pool decks, steps, sloped walks and anywhere barefoot children run. Film sealers get slick when wet. If you want color there, add the anti-slip grit the maker sells to the final coat, or choose a natural finish.

blocks.h3: Choosing by finish, traffic and climate

blocks.p: Hot, sunny climates add a twist. UV and heat age acrylic films faster, so sun-baked areas need recoating sooner than shaded ones, and you should seal early in the day before dark pavers get hot.

sections.h: What Weather Do You Need to Apply Water-Based Paver Sealer?

blocks.p: Water-based acrylics do not simply dry; they coalesce. The water leaves and the resin particles fuse. Cold air keeps the particles from softening enough to fuse, and humid air keeps the water from leaving. Either way the film can end up soft or milky. That is why these labels are so specific about temperature and humidity.

blocks.h3: Hot and humid climates, including Florida

blocks.p: In the Gulf states the problem is the reverse of the North: heat, afternoon storms and heavy morning dew. Seal mid-morning once the dew has burned off, finish before the pavers get hot to the touch and skip days with an afternoon storm in the forecast. Turn off irrigation for at least a day. Many Florida pool-deck owners favor penetrants or low-sheen acrylics because they stay cooler underfoot and less slippery.

A paver that looks dry can still release water from below after a wash or a rainy week, and that vapor pushing through a fresh film causes whitening. Wait 24 hours after washing, 48 in cool or humid weather, and tape a square of plastic down overnight; condensation underneath means wait longer.

sections.h: Can You Put Water-Based Sealer Over Old Sealer or Polymeric Sand?

blocks.h3: Find out what is already there

blocks.p: Splash water on the pavers. Beading on a dry, untreated-looking surface suggests an old penetrant. A sheen, flaking or a plastic feel means an acrylic film. Water that soaks in and darkens the paver at once means any old sealer is mostly gone.

Water-based acrylic often bonds poorly to sound solvent acrylic, which is slick and non-porous to it, and peeling within a season is the usual result. Either stay with a compatible solvent product or strip the old coat completely before switching. Water-based over water-based is generally fine after a thorough cleaning. A penetrant cannot soak through any film, so films have to come off first.

Polymeric sand must cure, often for several days to a few weeks depending on brand and weather, before sealer goes on top, and some makers list approved sealer types. Water-based sealer is usually the safer pairing, since strong solvents can soften some polymer binders. Read the sand bag first.

Seal a small hidden patch, let it cure several days, press masking tape onto it and pull sharply. Flakes on the tape mean poor adhesion. Ten minutes of testing can save a weekend of stripping. For poured concrete next to the pavers, our [concrete driveway sealer reviews](/best-concrete-driveway-sealer-reviews/) cover slab products, which are formulated a little differently.

sections.h: Which Sealer Works for Pool Pavers and Porcelain Pavers?

blocks.p: Around a pool you want three things: no extra slip, no peeling where chlorinated or salt water splashes, and a surface that stays comfortable barefoot. A water-based penetrant such as Siloxa-Tek 8500 or Eagle Natural Seal ticks all three. If you want color, use a low-sheen acrylic with anti-slip grit in the final coat and keep splash-out off the fresh coat until it cures.

blocks.h3: Can a sealer change the color of pool pavers?

blocks.p: Not really. A clear sealer can only deepen the existing color; an enhancer darkens it a shade or two. Changing the color itself takes a tinted coating or stain, and opaque film coatings on pool decks tend to peel where water sits. If longevity without peeling is the goal, a penetrating enhancer that soaks in usually outlasts any surface coating.

Porcelain is fired to very low absorption, so a penetrating sealer has almost nowhere to go and film sealers struggle to grip it. Most porcelain pavers need no face sealing at all; check the paver maker's care sheet. The joints are what need attention, and a jointing compound or polymeric product rated for porcelain is the fix.
Clay pavers absorb less than concrete, so thin coats of a penetrant or a light enhancer work best. Our [brick sealer guide](/best-brick-sealer-reviews/) explains why breathability matters on clay.

sections.h: How Much Water-Based Paver Sealer Do You Need, and How Long Does It Last?

blocks.p: Smooth, dense concrete pavers might cover 150 to 250 square feet per gallon per coat; tumbled or porous pavers drop to 80 to 120. Flooding joint sand can add 25 percent or more to the first coat. Penetrants usually go on as one saturating coat over a similar or slightly larger area.
Buy every pail of a color-enhancing product from the same batch so the sheen and color match across the patio.

Water-based acrylic films typically last about two to four years on a patio, less in hot sun, traffic lanes and driveways. Penetrants often carry longer life claims from their makers. The warning sign is the same for both: water soaks in and darkens the paver instead of beading.

Sweep often, rinse spills before they set and use a pH-neutral paver cleaner rather than acids or bleach; our [driveway cleaner guide](/best-driveway-cleaner/) lists gentle options. When the coat wears, clean and apply one thin maintenance coat of the same product. Do not add a coat every year, or the build-up will whiten and peel. In winter, use a gentler de-icer from our [ice melt for concrete](/best-ice-melt-for-concrete/) rankings so you do not wear out the sealer early.

mistakes: Water-based acrylic needs warmth to fuse into a clear film, and evening dew lands just as the film is most vulnerable. Start late morning on a dry day so the coat cures in rising temperatures, and postpone if the night is forecast to drop into the forties.

A solvent film can be re-melted to fix a bad coat. A cured water-based film generally cannot, so a cloudy or streaky coat usually means stripping. Plan as if there is no undo: thin coats, dry pavers, a good forecast and a test patch first.

A joint-stabilizing sealer can only bind sand that is dry and full. Flooding wet or sunken joints wastes product and leaves sand that washes out at the next storm. Refill the joints, sweep the faces clean, wait a full dry day, then flood.
Coating over an old solvent film

Water-based sealer often fails to bond to an intact solvent acrylic, and peeling follows within a season. Check what is on the pavers first, then either stay with a compatible solvent product or strip completely. A masking-tape test on a small patch confirms it.
Sealing too soon over new polymeric sand

Polymeric sand needs to cure before any sealer goes on top, and the time varies by brand and weather. Seal too early and you can trap moisture in the joints, haze the joint lines or weaken the bond. Follow the minimum wait printed on the sand bag.
bottomLine: Foundation Armor WB25 is the water-based pick for a wet look, Techniseal Matte Finish for pavers that should look untouched, SEK Surebond SB-6000 or Blok-Guard when joint sand keeps washing out, Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 for snow and salt, and Eagle Natural Seal when the budget is tight. The product matters less than the conditions: seal clean, fully dry pavers in thin coats on a warm, dry day with no rain or dew in the forecast, and a water-based sealer will cure clear and last as long as its label promises.

faqs.q: What is the best water based paver sealer?
faqs.a: Foundation Armor WB25 is the best water based paver sealer for a wet look, and Techniseal Matte Finish is the best for a natural look with no sheen. For snow and salt, a water-based penetrant such as Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 lasts better on driveways. For loose joint sand, choose SEK Surebond SB-6000 or Rain Guard Blok-Guard.

faqs.q: Is water based paver sealer as durable as solvent based?
faqs.a: Close, for stain resistance and water repellency. Solvent acrylics still give a deeper gloss and can be re-melted to fix mistakes, while water-based acrylics usually need stripping. Water-based penetrants are a standard choice on bridges and parking decks and hold up well. Prep, thin coats and weather matter more to durability than the carrier.

faqs.q: Will a water based sealer give pavers a wet look?
faqs.a: Yes, a water-based wet-look acrylic such as Foundation Armor WB25 deepens color and adds a satin-to-semi-gloss sheen, usually a little softer than a solvent product. Two thin coats look better than one heavy coat. Penetrating water-based sealers do not create a wet look at all; they leave the paver looking unchanged.

faqs.q: Why did my water based paver sealer turn white?
faqs.a: Moisture, almost always. The pavers were damp, the coat was too thick, humidity was high or dew settled on the film before it cured. Light haze sometimes clears after several warm, dry days. Heavy or lasting haze on a water-based acrylic usually needs a stripper and a fresh, thinner coat on a better day.

faqs.q: Is water based paver sealer safe around pets and plants?
faqs.a: It is far lower in VOCs and odor than solvent sealer, which makes it the better choice near gardens, pools and pets. It is still a chemical coating, so keep pets and children off until it cures, avoid overspray on plants and read the safety data sheet. Once fully cured, a sealed patio is fine for normal use.

faqs.q: Does water based sealer stabilize paver joint sand?
faqs.a: A water-based acrylic made for pavers, such as SEK Surebond SB-6000 or Blok-Guard, binds the top of ordinary joint sand when the joints are full and dry as you flood them. Penetrating repellents do not bind sand. For joints that wash out badly, re-sanding with polymeric sand is the stronger fix.

faqs.q: What is the coldest temperature to apply water based paver sealer?
faqs.a: About 50 degrees Fahrenheit for both air and paver surface on most labels, with temperatures holding or rising for several hours afterward. Cold slows the curing process and raises the risk of a soft or cloudy film. In spring and fall, seal during the warmest part of a dry day and skip days with frost forecast overnight.
